conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in last night with vomiting and abdominal pain during your tube feed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started around 10:30 PM. I was on my usual feed, but suddenly got sharp pain and started vomiting. It felt just like my last flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. No fever, chills, or blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. My J-tube is clear, and I’ve had bowel movements. It’s just the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. Your exam shows mild tenderness but no signs of blockage. We checked labs—your bicarbonate is a bit low at 19, and lactate is slightly elevated at 2.3, which suggests mild dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve been having these flares more often lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not dangerous right now. The dehydration is mild. We’re giving you IV fluids and medications to calm your stomach—Zofran, Reglan, Ativan, and a little morphine for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s the same combo that helped before. I hope it works again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it usually does. We’ll keep your tube feeds off for now and restart slowly once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little tired, but the pain is much better. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your repeat vitals are stable—BP 112/73, pulse 81. We’ll start clear liquids by mouth and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure you can keep fluids down and tolerate your tube feeds again. This usually takes a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well with clear liquids. We’re going to restart your J-tube feeds at a low rate—68 mL/hr—for the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought we slowed it to 90 before. Is 68 safer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered it from 90 to see if that reduced flares. But this episode happened even at 68, so we’re not sure the rate is the only factor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing them then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastroparesis is idiopathic—no clear cause. No diabetes, no nerve damage, no cancer. The gastric emptying scan showed 48% retention at 4 hours, which confirms delayed emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And there’s nothing else they can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At this point, the focus is on managing symptoms. You’re followed by Dr. Patel at the GI clinic—they’ve said no further interventions are likely to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish it didn’t keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep using the same meds that work—ondansetron, Tigan, lorazepam as needed. And stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. Your labs this morning look better—bicarbonate still 19, but kidney function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. First, we’ll increase your tube feeds back to your regular rate and watch you for a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I take levothyroxine at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve been giving it every night. Your thyroid levels are stable, so no changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to do a formal enteral feeding infusion at 90 mL/hr now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. No nausea so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you tolerated the full feed without issues. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been so anxious about these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your anxiety and depression are being managed with citalopram and lorazepam as needed. Keep using them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my appointment with Dr. Patel in two weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. They’ll monitor your gastroparesis long-term. No changes to your other meds—vitamin D, omeprazole, all stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check—you’re still feeling well, no pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your discharge labs are stable. We’ll send you home with instructions to continue your meds and follow up with Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your PRN meds—ondansetron, Tigan, lorazepam. If it doesn’t settle within a few hours, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be out by 10 AM.
